title: Research
text:
Biomedicine can now generate molecular data at extraordinary scale. What remains hard is knowing which signals are real, which conclusions will generalise, and which predictions are trustworthy enough to act on.
My research tackles that problem where the stakes are highest and the data are thinnest: antimicrobial resistance (AMR). I build models that report not only what they predict, but when, why and for whom that prediction should be trusted, and I treat their failures as information about hidden biology rather than as noise.

    B --> C["Disagreement flagged<br/>(genotype vs phenotype,<br/>model vs sensitivity analysis)"]
    C --> D["Decision-grade evidence<br/>for researchers and policy"]

title: Research
section: 1. Evidence synthesis under heterogeneity
text:
1. Evidence synthesis under heterogeneity
The question: how do we combine surveillance data that differ in laboratory, method, breakpoint and year, without pretending they are the same or throwing away what sparse settings can teach us?
What I have done:

Argus AI: a Bayesian hierarchical synthesis of 4.95 million isolate–drug observations (71 countries, 44 species, ten antibiotics, 2004–2024), linked to global AMR R&D investment, with partial pooling and isolate-weighted and country-balanced sensitivity analyses. Global AMR R&D Hub Cross-Domain Award, 2026 Vivli AMR Surveillance Data Challenge.
ResistAI+: Bayesian change-point modelling, MIC-creep analysis and posterior-predictive forecasting across multi-country data. Finalist, top 10% of 100+ teams, 2025 Vivli AMR Surveillance Global Data Challenge.

title: Research
section: 2. Disagreement as a signal
text:
2. Disagreement as a signal
The question: when phenotype says resistant and the genome says susceptible, is that an error, a new mechanism, or a limit of the method? Most pipelines quietly choose one source. I think the disagreement itself should be modelled.
What I have done:

NaijaResist: a prototype that reconciles phenotypic resistance, gene burden, cross-species transfer and organism-level threat, flagging discordance so it is visible and reviewable, alongside machine-learning resistance prediction and trend analysis for Nigeria.
AGARI E. coli data integration (BioSeq, Africa CDC / ASLM): contributed to a proposal that defines AMR results at the highest justified resolution (family, allele, mutation, mechanism) with call-resolution state and tool, database and version provenance, a PHA4GE hAMRonization mapping, and genotype–phenotype discordance flags that retain both sources.

title: Research
section: 3. Trustworthy computational discovery
text:
3. Trustworthy computational discovery
The question: a ranked list of candidate molecules is only useful if we know how far to trust the ranking. How do we build discovery pipelines whose reliability can be examined at each step, so that a high computational score cannot rescue an implausible molecule?
What I have done:

Morph-HSV: resistance-aware antiviral prioritisation (team lead)
2026 Shanghai Computational Biology competition, preliminary round · Team of four · Code
The task was to rank 100 non-nucleoside candidates against HSV-1 DNA polymerase for experimental testing, while accounting for resistance-associated variants and chemical feasibility. I led a team that treated this as a multi-stage prioritisation problem instead of a single-score virtual screen.





flowchart LR
    A["~22,000 compounds<br/>literature, docking evidence,<br/>ChEMBL and similarity mining"] --> B["1,004 molecules<br/>541 scaffolds<br/>scaffold-aware QSAR"]
    B --> C["~5 million molecules screened<br/>Top 1,000"]
    C --> D["374 after property<br/>and feasibility filters"]
    D --> E["Glide HTVS/XP re-docking<br/>against 8VQ2"]
    E --> F["Ranked Top 100<br/>with resistance-variant checks"]







Scaffold-aware evaluation. Models (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, Ridge) were validated on non-overlapping scaffold groups, so that performance reflects prediction on new chemistry rather than near-copies of training molecules. The production model reached a mean R² of 0.55 ± 0.07 (RMSE 0.74, MAE 0.59) across ten randomised scaffold splits. I report this deliberately conservative figure because it is the honest one.
Explicit gates, not one score. The final ranking combines QSAR prediction, XP docking, synthetic accessibility, drug-likeness, physicochemical and structural-alert criteria, and scaffold-diversity control, with matched re-docking against wild-type and the W781V, N815S and Y941H resistance variants where available.
Auditability. Large-library screening preserved identifiers and failed-structure logs, and top candidates received manual pose review.
Status: [PRELIMINARY ROUND SUBMITTED. ADD OUTCOME ONLY WHEN ANNOUNCED AND ACCURATE.] These are computational predictions; none has yet been experimentally tested.



Earlier discovery work

First-author study of natural-product inhibitors of InhA, a tuberculosis target, combining molecular descriptors, model evaluation, docking and molecular dynamics (Biology Methods and Protocols, 2026).
First-author study of 4-quinolone ligands for GRK5 using message-passing neural networks, docking and molecular dynamics (Egyptian Journal of Medical Human Genetics, 2025).
Winner, 2025 Advanced CADD Machine-Learning Drug Discovery Challenge, with leading enrichment factor and error performance in an international West African cohort.

title: Research
section: 4. From molecular signal to clinical outcome
text:
4. From molecular signal to clinical outcome
The question: why do patients with seemingly similar molecular profiles have very different outcomes?
What I have done: built multi-omics survival models integrating transcriptomic, whole-genome, immune and clinical data, and found with Cox proportional-hazards modelling that low HLA class I expression predicts poorer outcomes. I also analysed RNA-seq and microarray cohorts (DESeq2, limma, GSEA) from a Sri Lankan nasopharyngeal carcinoma study. This thread taught me to ask what a model is missing, not only what it captures.

title: Projects
text:
Most tools for antimicrobial resistance (AMR) tell you what has happened. The ones I build also tell you how sure they are, where their data run out, and where the sources disagree. The projects below follow that idea from global surveillance to a single protein pocket.
All three surveillance systems were developed at the Helix Biogen Institute. The dashboards run on free hosting, so one that has been idle may take around 30 seconds to wake. Please give it a moment.

title: Projects
section: Argus AI: where the threat and the response fail to meet
text:
Argus AI: where the threat and the response fail to meet
Global AMR R&D Hub Cross-Domain Award, 2026 Vivli AMR Surveillance Data Challenge · Project lead, Helix Biogen Institute · Open dashboard

The problem
AMR burden, resistance mechanisms, surveillance capacity, research funding and drug-development activity are usually assessed separately. That makes it hard to see whether the greatest threats are getting proportionate scientific and financial attention.



What I built
A Bayesian hierarchical evidence synthesis of 4.95 million isolate–drug observations (71 countries, 44 species, ten antibiotics, 2004–2024), combined with global AMR R&D investment data. The framework integrates:

Bayesian burden–funding alignment, with partial pooling so sparse countries borrow strength without being treated as identical
Isolate-weighted and country-balanced sensitivity analyses, so conclusions do not hinge on one modelling choice
Resistance-mechanism intelligence and drug-pipeline performance
Surveillance-equity diagnostics and policy-effect analysis
Citation-grounded AI evidence retrieval, with versioned data lineage so every claim can be traced to its source



What it shows
Where resistance burden, therapeutic vulnerability, scientific attention and investment are most dangerously misaligned, and how much that conclusion depends on how the data are weighted.

title: Projects
section: ResistAI+: resistance with error bars and a forecast
text:
ResistAI+: resistance with error bars and a forecast
Finalist, top 10% of 100+ teams, 2025 Vivli AMR Surveillance Global Data Challenge · Team lead, data analysis and deployment, Helix Biogen Institute · Open dashboard

The problem
Most AMR platforms describe where resistance has occurred. Few say how confidently it can be estimated, why it may be changing, or where it may emerge next.


What I built
An interactive platform on Pfizer ATLAS data (2004–2023) that combines:

Bayesian hierarchical modelling of temporal and geographic variation in non-susceptibility
Change-point detection and MIC-creep analysis for levofloxacin, meropenem and linezolid
Resistance-risk prediction and posterior-predictive, time-to-threshold forecasting
Causal analysis using directed acyclic graphs
Policy-priority analytics across countries



What it shows
Not only which resistance patterns exist, but how much each estimate can be trusted, when trends shifted, and which settings deserve attention first.

Limits I am explicit about: the causal graphs encode assumptions, and the forecasts are conditional on trends continuing. The dashboard shows intervals, not single numbers, for this reason.

title: Projects
section: NaijaResist: prediction that shows where the evidence disagrees
text:
NaijaResist: prediction that shows where the evidence disagrees
Prototype · Project lead and architect, Helix Biogen Institute · Open dashboard

The problem
Surveillance in Nigeria is fragmented across hospitals, laboratories, pathogens and regions. Where phenotypic resistance and genetic evidence disagree, most pipelines quietly pick one and move on. And without integration, emerging hotspots are hard to see.


What I built
A prototype AMR intelligence system for Nigeria that combines two things usually kept apart:

Prediction and trends: machine-learning resistance prediction, geographic and temporal trend analysis, epidemiological forecasting and pathogen–antibiotic profiling
Genotype–phenotype reconciliation: phenotypic resistance, gene burden, cross-species transfer and organism-level threat are reconciled, and discordance is flagged so that it is visible and reviewable rather than hidden



What it shows
Where the models and the genomic evidence agree, where they diverge, and which divergences deserve an expert’s attention. Often that is where the most interesting biology, or the most important data-quality problem, sits.

section: Natural-product inhibitors of InhA, a tuberculosis target
text:
Natural-product inhibitors of InhA, a tuberculosis target
First and corresponding author · Biology Methods and Protocols (2026) · Paper · [GITHUB-LINK]
I developed a machine-learning-driven QSAR and structural-bioinformatics workflow for screening natural products against InhA. It integrates molecular descriptors, model evaluation, docking and molecular dynamics. The aim was a pipeline in which each step’s reliability can be examined, not only a ranked list of candidates.



Structural stability of the top-ranked hits over a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation. RMSD of the InhA apo form (black) and four top-hit complexes (LTS0023082, LTS0064866, LTS0078946, LTS0161715) settles after roughly 40 ns and stays within a narrow band of about 2 to 3 Å for the remainder of the run, comparable to the unliganded protein. title: About
text:
Every antibiotic ever made is an argument with evolution, and evolution has had four billion years of practice. Resistance is what it looks like when that argument is being lost: slowly, quietly, one hospital ward at a time.
The data that should tell us where we are losing are patchy, unevenly collected, and often thinnest in the places where infection hits hardest. A model trained on such data can sound certain and be wrong. So I build the other kind: models that say not only what they predict, but how far, when, and for whom that prediction can be trusted.
I am Godswill Imolele Anthony, a computational biologist working on explainable, uncertainty-aware AI for antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and antimicrobial discovery. I am seeking a PhD where this work can grow into a rigorous, independent research programme.

title: About
section: Three questions that drive my work
text:
Three questions that drive my work
1. Which signals are real? Surveillance data are heterogeneous: different laboratories, methods, breakpoints and years. Partial pooling lets sparse settings borrow strength from richer ones without pretending they are the same. In Argus AI, I checked the conclusions with isolate-weighted and country-balanced sensitivity analyses, so the results do not depend on one modelling choice.
2. Where do predictions stop being trustworthy? Biomarkers and models often lose validity when they cross ancestries, health systems or pathogen lineages. I treat that failure as information about hidden biological structure rather than as noise to be averaged away.
3. Can a model show its disagreement? Phenotype says resistant; the genome says susceptible. Most pipelines quietly pick one. In NaijaResist, I keep both sources, flag the discordance, and make it reviewable, because that disagreement is often where the biology is.

title: About
section: How I got here
text:
How I got here
I began at the bench. As a research assistant at the Nigerian Institute of Medical Research, I ran more than 200 ELISA and TIA assays and 20+ Western blots, and managed mouse colonies under Good Laboratory Practice. That taught me something many modellers never learn: how data are made, and how many small decisions sit between a living system and a number in a spreadsheet.
At the Helix Biogen Institute, I moved into bioinformatics and statistical modelling. I integrated transcriptomic, immune, whole-genome and clinical data into survival models, finding that low HLA class I expression predicts poorer outcomes, and I led a four-month metagenomics project with nine junior researchers.
From there, the thread tightened around one question: how do we make computational biology honest enough to guide decisions about infection? That led to AMR surveillance, to Bayesian forecasting, and to machine-learning discovery of new inhibitors, including a first-author study of natural-product inhibitors of InhA, a tuberculosis target, published in Biology Methods and Protocols (2026). I also work as a bioinformatics associate on infection genomics and metagenomics projects, including a proposal to integrate E. coli genomic surveillance into the African Genomes Archive for Response and Insights (AGARI).

title: About
section: Why Africa is a scientific argument, not only an equity one
text:
Why Africa is a scientific argument, not only an equity one
African populations and pathogens hold some of the greatest genetic diversity on Earth, yet they are underrepresented in the datasets that shape biomedical knowledge. That is an issue of fairness. It is also a discovery problem. Models built on narrow populations carry assumptions they cannot see, and the cases where those models fail teach us what is actually universal and what only seemed to be.
Where data are sparse, quantifying uncertainty is not a luxury; it is the only responsible way to reason. That is why I build from Nigeria, and why I think this setting can produce methods the rest of the world will need.

title: About
section: What I am looking for in a PhD
text:
What I am looking for in a PhD
I want to train in a group that takes both rigorous statistics and real biological data seriously. Specifically, I hope to:

Develop calibrated, transportable models for resistance and drug discovery that hold up across populations and pathogen lineages
Strengthen my foundations in Bayesian inference, causal reasoning and probabilistic machine learning
Work with pathogen genomics and experimental collaborators so that predictions are tested against biology, not only benchmarks
Build open, reproducible tools that other researchers, including those in low-resource settings, can reuse

I bring a record of delivering end to end: from messy multi-country data, through models with quantified uncertainty, to systems people can actually use. I am looking for the mentorship to take that to the next level.
